about: LL100 Legal Studies Skills is a compulsory, non-assessed and non-credit-bearing course for first-year LSE LLB in Laws (and BA Anthropology and Law) students. In 2026/27 it consists of 10 hours of classes in Autumn Term, building six skills: active reading and note-making, independent research, evaluating legal materials, structured written argument, applying law to problems and reflecting on your own development. The course guide lists no formative or summative assessment, and its reading is drawn from the first-year core law courses. This guide explains the course and gives practical, factual guidance on the skills; it does not invent a syllabus.
topics: What LL100 is and how it works
Active reading and note-making: cases and statutes
Independent research and evaluating legal materials
Structured writing: essays, problem questions and referencing

notes.body:
LL100 Legal Studies Skills is a compulsory course for first-year students on the LSE LLB in Laws (and the BA in Anthropology and Law). The facts below come from the 2026/27 course guide.

What it is
- A non-assessed, non-credit-bearing course designed to build the skills needed to study law.
- Taught through 10 hours of classes in Autumn Term, with a reading week in Week 6.
- The guide lists no formative coursework and no summative assessment, so there is no exam or mark for LL100 itself.
- The reading is drawn from the weekly material for the first-year core law courses, so you are not expected to read extra texts; a reading guide is provided at the start of the course.

The six learning outcomes
By the end of the course you should be able to:
- read legal material actively and make comprehensive working notes;
- carry out independent, self-directed research;
- critically evaluate a range of legal materials;
- write clear, well-structured and reasoned arguments supported by evidence;
- identify and apply the relevant law to a problem scenario in a structured, methodical way;
- assess and reflect on your own skills development, identify areas to improve and choose suitable ways to do so.

Why it matters even though it is not assessed
The skills LL100 builds are the ones assessed in the first-year core courses. For example, Contract Law and Criminal Law are each assessed by a three-hour exam in 2026/27, and Introduction to Legal Systems requires a formative essay of up to 1,500 words. Treat LL100 classes as practice for those, using the same cases and materials.

How to get the most from it
- Do the core-course reading the class is built around before you arrive, so you can practise skills on material you have already met.
- Bring your notes and drafts; the value of a skills class comes from applying advice to your own work.
- Keep a short skills log: after each class, note one thing you did well, one thing to improve and one concrete step (for example, "rewrite my case notes for Gibson v Manchester City Council using the template").
- Act on feedback from your core-course formative assessments and link it back to the LL100 outcomes.

Exam tips: there is no LL100 exam, but the best preparation for your core-course exams is to practise these skills under timed conditions on past-style questions from those courses.

Active reading means reading with a purpose and recording what matters, rather than highlighting everything. Law students read three main kinds of primary material: judgments, statutes and secondary commentary.

Anatomy of a reported case
- Case name: in civil cases, claimant v defendant (on appeal the order may change). In criminal cases, R (the Crown) v defendant.
- Neutral citation: the court's own reference, independent of any publisher, e.g. [2016] UKSC 8 (the 8th UK Supreme Court judgment of 2016). Others include EWCA Civ, EWCA Crim, and High Court divisions such as EWHC (KB), (Ch), (Comm) and (Admin).
- Law report citation: where the case is printed, e.g. [1998] AC 1 (Appeal Cases) or [1991] 1 QB 1 (Queen's Bench). Other common series are the Weekly Law Reports (WLR) and the All England Law Reports (All ER). The official Law Reports (AC, QB/KB, Ch, Fam) are preferred where available.
- Square brackets mean the year is needed to find the volume; round brackets mean the volumes are numbered independently and the year is just the date of the decision, e.g. (1871) LR 6 QB 597.
- The headnote is the reporter's summary. It is useful for orientation but is not part of the judgment and is not authoritative.

What to record in case notes
- Court, date and judges (and any dissents).
- Material facts, in a few lines.
- The legal issue(s).
- The decision and the reasoning, distinguishing the ratio (what was necessary for the decision) from obiter remarks.
- How the case fits with others: followed, distinguished, criticised or overruled.
- Your own evaluation: is the reasoning convincing, and what are its social effects?

Reading statutes
- Note the short title and year, then the structure: Parts, sections, subsections and paragraphs (e.g. Theft Act 1968, s 5(4)).
- Check the version in force: legislation.gov.uk shows amendments and whether provisions have been commenced. New Acts often come into force in stages by regulations.
- Look at definitions sections and any explanatory notes, remembering that explanatory notes are only an aid to meaning.

Note-making methods
- Make notes in your own words, organised by issue rather than by reading.
- Build a running "map" for each topic: the rule, its leading authorities, its exceptions and the main debates.
- Keep a separate list of questions you could not answer, to raise in classes.

Exam tips: in your core-course exams, the cases you can use well are the ones you have noted actively, with facts, ratio and a view of your own.

notes.h: Independent research and evaluating legal materials
notes.body:
LL100 aims to make you an independent researcher. That means knowing where to look, how to judge what you find, and how to keep it up to date.

Where to find the law
- Legislation: legislation.gov.uk (the official, free source of UK legislation, showing amendments and commencement).
- Judgments: Find Case Law, run by The National Archives (launched in April 2022), publishes judgments of the UK Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, High Court and some tribunals free of charge. BAILII is another free source.
- Subscription databases provided through the library, such as Westlaw and Lexis, add law reports, case histories (showing whether a case has been followed or overruled), journal articles and practitioner texts.
- Secondary sources: textbooks (start with the course's recommended textbook), journal articles and law reform reports (e.g. from the Law Commission).

Evaluating sources
Ask of every source:
- Authority: is it primary law (statute, judgment) or commentary? Which court decided it, and is it binding or persuasive?
- Currency: is it still good law? Has the statute been amended or the case overruled? A textbook may be out of date on recent changes.
- Reliability: who wrote it, and for what purpose? Peer-reviewed articles and official publications are more reliable than anonymous websites or student essays.
- Argument: does the author present evidence fairly, and what assumptions or values drive their view?

A simple research routine
- Start from the reading list and textbook to understand the topic.
- Identify the leading primary sources (statutes and cases) and read them.
- Check that each is current using a database's case history or legislation.gov.uk.
- Read two or three articles that take different views, and note their arguments.
- Record full citations as you go, so referencing is easy later.

Using generative AI tools
Follow LSE's and your course's current guidance on whether and how such tools may be used. Never rely on them for legal authorities without checking the original source: they can produce plausible but non-existent cases or wrong citations.

Exam tips: in essays, show evaluation by weighing sources (for example, majority versus dissent, or an author's argument against later case law), not just listing them.

notes.h: Writing essays and answering problem questions
notes.body:
LL100's learning outcomes include writing clear, structured, evidence-based arguments and applying law to problems methodically. These are the two main forms of law assessment.

Essays
- Answer the question set: identify the claim or quotation, its key terms and what it asks you to evaluate.
- State your answer (thesis) in the introduction and say how you will argue for it.
- Organise paragraphs around points of argument, not around cases. Each paragraph should make a point, support it with authority or evidence, and explain how it advances your thesis.
- Deal with the strongest counter-arguments.
- Conclude by answering the question directly; do not introduce new material.

Problem questions
A common structure is IRAC (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion):
- Issue: identify each legal issue raised by the facts, party by party.
- Rule: state the relevant law accurately with authority (statute section or case).
- Application: apply the rule to the specific facts, considering arguments on both sides where the facts are unclear.
- Conclusion: give a reasoned conclusion on each issue, with your level of confidence.
Tips: take the issues in a logical order (for example, formation before breach and remedies in contract; actus reus, mens rea, then defences in criminal law). Do not write out everything you know about a topic; use only the law the facts call for.

Referencing
- Legal writing in the UK usually uses OSCOLA (the Oxford University Standard for the Citation of Legal Authorities), which uses footnotes. The fifth edition was published in March 2026. Follow LSE Law School's instructions on which style and edition to use.
- Typical OSCOLA features: case names in italics; neutral citation before the law report citation; statutes cited by short title and year without a comma; minimal punctuation.
- Referencing is part of academic integrity: always acknowledge where ideas and words come from.

Reflecting on your skills
The sixth outcome is reflection. After each piece of formative work, compare the feedback with these outcomes, pick one or two priorities, and decide how to work on them (for example, practising timed problem answers or rewriting an introduction).

Exam tips: plan before you write, even in timed exams; a clear structure earns more credit than extra material.

questions.q: What does the citation [2017] UKSC 67 tell you?
options: It was decided by the Court of Appeal in 2017
It is the 67th judgment of the UK Supreme Court in 2017
It was the 67th case heard by the House of Lords
The case is reported on page 67 of the 2017 Appeal Cases
questions.why: A neutral citation gives the year, the court and the judgment's number in that court's sequence. Treating 67 as a page number confuses a neutral citation with a law report citation such as [2017] AC 67. UKSC denotes the Supreme Court; the Court of Appeal's neutral citations use EWCA Civ or EWCA Crim. The House of Lords stopped sitting judicially in 2009, and its judgments used UKHL.

questions.q: Why is it a mistake to quote a case's headnote as if it were the court's reasoning?
options: Because the headnote is the law reporter's summary, not part of the judgment, and may be inaccurate
Because headnotes are written by the judges and are too informal to cite
Because the headnote summarises counsel's arguments, not the decision
questions.why: The headnote is the law reporter's editorial summary and has no authority; the judgment itself must be read for the ratio. Headnotes are written by the reporter, not by the judges, so attributing them to the court is the mistake. In the official Law Reports a summary of counsel's arguments is printed separately after the headnote; the headnote summarises the decision. 'Obiter' describes parts of a judgment; a headnote is not part of the judgment at all, so calling it obiter misdescribes it.

questions.q: In the IRAC method for problem questions, what belongs in the 'Application' stage?
options: Restating the facts of the problem without analysis
Applying the stated legal rule to the particular facts, including arguments both ways where facts are unclear
A general essay on the history of the area of law
Listing every case on the reading list
questions.why: Application is where marks are earned by linking rule to facts. A history of the area is essay material and belongs in a problem answer only if it helps. Listing cases without applying them shows memory, not analysis. Restating the facts adds nothing; the facts must be analysed against the rule.

questions.q: List five things you should record in a case note, and explain why distinguishing ratio from obiter matters. (5 marks)
markScheme: Court, date and judges (and any dissent)
Decision and reasoning (ratio vs obiter); later treatment (followed/distinguished/overruled)
Why it matters: only the ratio binds later courts; obiter is persuasive only; affects how the case can be used in arguments
questions.modelAnswer: A useful case note records: the court, date and judges, including any dissents; the material facts in brief; the legal issue or issues; the decision and the reasoning; and how later cases have treated it (followed, distinguished or overruled), plus your own evaluation. Distinguishing ratio from obiter matters because only the ratio, the reasoning necessary for the decision, binds later courts under the doctrine of precedent. Obiter remarks are only persuasive. Knowing which is which tells you how strongly the case supports an argument and whether it can be distinguished.
